source.title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

record.tranche_reason: The post reports probing results about linear decodability of arbitrary XORs in an LLM, but does not test whether sparse features are stored in superposition, how their geometry depends on sparsity or importance, or any specific version listed.
record.gate_note: The post's XOR probing results are recorded as findings about LLM representations under fits_no_version. Its arguments about superposition and capacity are not experimental tests of the listed versions. Values used only for setup, including the 80/20 split and model dimensions, are not result rows.
record.test_reason: The post probes LLaMA-2-13B for linear decodability of XORs of binary features. It does not measure superposition geometry, capacity allocation, neuron polysemanticity, SAE features, or feature dimensionality. Superposition and capacity appear only in arguments and footnotes (e.g. 'the model must allocate additional capacity'), not as tested results.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with three corrections. The author concludes that RAX (linear representation of arbitrary XORs) held in every case checked, and finds this surprising and confusing. The reset-network result is taken to rule out the 'represented by chance in high dimensions' explanation. The author puts most weight on the idea that XORs are decoded by aggregating noisy signals from features correlated with a AND b. He also argues that RAX is a bad sign for probe generalization and for interpretability more broadly.
record.recipe_differences: The post uses linear probes on LLM activations to test XOR decodability; it does not reproduce the toy-network feature-superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The post reports variations in feature construction and token position, and separately reports that XOR decodability did not beat the OR baseline in the reset network.

fits_no_version.finding: In LLaMA-2-13B (layer 14, period token), linear probes classify XORs of arbitrary binary features (has_alice XOR has_not, has_not XOR label, has_true XOR has_banana) with perfect or near-perfect test accuracy. This holds even after per-group centering removes has_not decodability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM residual streams make XORs of arbitrary, apparently useless features linearly decodable.

fits_no_version.finding: In a weight-shuffled (reset) LLaMA-2-13B, token-level features stay decodable, but the has_alice XOR has_not probe does not beat the .75 OR baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: XOR decodability depends on learned weights, not on chance high-dimensional mixing of token features.

fits_no_version.finding: Basic features appear in PCs 1 and 3; the XOR appears only from PC 6 onward.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: XOR directions carry less variance (are less salient) than basic feature directions.

record.problems: The post gives no per-case accuracy numbers or uncertainty estimates for its positive XOR findings. It reports a reset-network comparison but no other control for the main findings. The post itself raises a possible train/test dependency in the cities data split.

untested.parts: Toy networks, sparsity-dependent transition, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, regular geometry; none studied.
Capacity competition and dedicated versus shared dimensions are argued about for XOR directions but not measured.
Polysemantic neurons arising without capacity pressure; no neuron-level analysis.
Spread of features across neurons and SAE recovery of sparse features; the post only uses linear probes on the residual stream.
Completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features; not studied.
One-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features; not studied.

record.verdict_notes: Rows are correctly linked to 'none'; no per-case accuracy numbers appear in the text (results are shown in figures). The comments include others' results: a failed replication at about 75% XOR accuracy (leogao), toy random-MLP experiments in which XOR appears only with redundant features (Fabien Roger), and Pythia-70m results (Dumas). These are not the author's results and do not bear on the listed versions. The author's own comment notes that the 80/20 split introduces train/test dependence, which explains below-50% accuracies.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, excess sparse features, overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Neuron polysemanticity, capacity competition, and dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.
Feature spread across neurons and recovery of sparse features with a dictionary or SAE.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.
